summary: This experimental memo replaces RFC 1409 to fix a typographical error in an example, and it defines a Telnet option for negotiating user authentication. It was later replaced by RFC 2941.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a corrected copy of an earlier paper about proving who you are when logging into a remote computer. One word in an example was wrong, so they published it again.

questions: how does telnet authentication option work
what authentication methods does telnet support
can telnet authentication prevent password theft
subtitle: A way to prove your identity over Telnet without sending passwords in the clear

tldr.problem: Telnet users had to type passwords, which were sent in plain text across the network, risking interception by attackers watching the connection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Telnet option that negotiates a common authentication method (such as Kerberos) between client and server, allowing both to exchange cryptographic credentials instead of passwords.
tldr.outcome: The option enables secure authentication over Telnet and supports automatic login without typing passwords. It was later superseded by SSH and other protocols.

today: RFC 1416 is an Experimental protocol that replaced RFC 1409 (fixing a typographical error in an example) and was itself superseded by RFC 2941. Although the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option was standardized, it never saw widespread deployment. The emergence of SSH (Secure Shell) in the late 1990s provided superior security and became the preferred way to access remote systems, rendering Telnet authentication largely obsolete.

sections.title: The Problem with Clear-Text Passwords
sections.content:
The Telnet protocol lets users log into remote systems, but it has a significant security weakness: users must type their passwords, which are transmitted in clear text across the network. If the connection passes through untrusted networks, an attacker watching the packets can steal the password.

RFC 1416 defines an AUTHENTICATION option for Telnet to solve this problem. The option provides a framework for exchanging authentication information securely, so passwords do not travel in the clear. Additionally, if the Telnet client has appropriate credentials, it can automatically send the authentication information without the user typing anything.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet sends everything you type, including passwords, where anyone watching the network can read it. This option lets you prove who you are with a secret code instead.

sections.title: Commands and Negotiation
sections.content:
The AUTHENTICATION option uses standard Telnet option negotiation. The client sends WILL AUTHENTICATION to indicate it will support authentication. The server sends DO AUTHENTICATION to request it. Once both sides agree, the server becomes free to request authentication information.

The negotiation defines two roles: the client (the side that made the active TCP connection) and the server (the side that listened). Only the server may send a SEND command listing the authentication types it accepts. Only the client may send an IS command with authentication data. The server may send a REPLY command to respond to the client's credentials. The client may also send a NAME command to specify which account on the remote host it wishes to use.
sections.plainLanguage: First the client and server agree to talk about authentication. Then the server asks for credentials, the client sends them, and the server says whether it worked.

sections.title: Authentication Types and Modifiers
sections.content:
The RFC defines several authentication types: NULL (no authentication), KERBEROS_V4, KERBEROS_V5, SPX, RSA, and LOKI. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains the list for future additions.

Each authentication type is accompanied by a modifier that specifies the direction and mode of authentication. The AUTH_WHO_MASK bit indicates whether the client authenticates to the server (CLIENT_TO_SERVER) or the server authenticates to the client (SERVER_TO_CLIENT). The AUTH_HOW_MASK bit indicates whether authentication is one-way (HOW_ONE_WAY) or mutual (HOW_MUTUAL), where mutual means both sides prove their identity to each other.

This creates four possible combinations: client authenticates to server one-way, server authenticates to client one-way, both authenticate to each other mutually with client first, or both authenticate mutually with server first. The server lists its preferred authentication types in order of preference when it sends the SEND command.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to prove who you are (Kerberos, RSA, etc.) can work one-way or both ways. The server picks which methods it trusts and asks the client to use one.

sections.title: Message Exchange Example
sections.content:
The RFC provides an example exchange using Kerberos authentication. The server requests KERBEROS_V4 with CLIENT|MUTUAL (mutual authentication with client first) or KERBEROS_V4 with CLIENT|ONE_WAY (one-way authentication) as a fallback.

The client responds with a NAME command specifying the username (e.g., 'joe') and then sends the authentication data in the IS command—in this case, a Kerberos ticket. The server verifies the ticket and replies with ACCEPT. For mutual authentication, the client then sends a CHALLENGE to verify the server's identity, and the server responds with a RESPONSE to prove it is genuine. Multiple exchanges of IS and REPLY commands may occur as needed for the chosen authentication scheme.

If the client does not support any of the offered authentication types, it should respond with NULL to indicate this. The server may then choose to close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks for credentials. The client sends them with the username. The server checks them and says yes or no. If both sides need to verify each other, they send more messages to do that.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC notes an important security consideration: during the authentication negotiation phase, before any authentication has occurred, neither side knows whether it is talking to the intended party. An intruder could attempt to negotiate the use of a weak authentication method, or one already compromised by the intruder. This means the choice of authentication method itself must be protected, or administrators must ensure that only strong methods are offered.

Despite this limitation, the AUTHENTICATION option is a significant improvement over sending passwords in clear text. By moving authentication out of the Telnet command stream and into a negotiated framework, the mechanism allows implementations to use strong cryptographic methods appropriate to the environment.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker could try to trick you into using a weak way of proving who you are. But even so, this is much safer than typing your password where everyone can see it.
